chapter_theme: The book's last twenty verses turn to conduct before the king, elders and other households, with a few rules of the funeral rite, of leavings and of the day of a rite, and close by naming the persons freed from ஆசாரம்.
structure_note: Verses 81-85 conduct at and toward the court; 86-89 and 91, 93-94, 97 courtesy and self-restraint; 87, 90, 92 ritual, purity and caste rules; 95 the four things to guard; 96 animals as models of keeping to one's work; 98-99 places not entered; 100 the nine exempt.

81.reading: The verse says that the upright who do not hold the office concerned do not enter by the back gate and do not look into the king's assembly or the women's quarters of the palace.
81.domain_note: those who move about the king's palace
81.nuance: The bar is tied to office: அவ்வத் தொழிற்குரிவர் அல்லா தவர் (read as தொழிற்குரியவர்) leaves the same doors open to those whose work lies there, so the rule is about trespass, not about the places being forbidden as such. செவ்வியார் may name the upright or those who watch for an opening; the reading takes the first.

items.claim: the back gate is not entered by those whose office it is not
the king's assembly is not looked into by those not called to it
the women's quarters of the palace are not looked into by those not serving there

82.reading: The verse says that those who count themselves wise do not take a seat near the place of the women, even when they have a very close claim of intimacy, because what pleases women turns out to be other than one supposes.
82.nuance: The reason given is a claim about women's liking, not about the men's desire, so the rule rests on a generalisation about women. Line 1 is hard: மகளிரி is likely மகளிர் miswritten, and whether வண்ண மகளிர் are the king's women (as the neighbouring verses would suggest) or any women of a house is not said.

norm.note: a rule of the period keeping men from sitting near women, justified by a claim about women's changeable liking

83.reading: The verse lists what those who mean to live long and to the end do not do: walk along in a row, stand treading on a shadow, speak by picking at another's talk in its midst, do what the town resents, or tell even the size of the king's army.
83.domain_note: those who live near the king and would keep their place
83.nuance: Whose shadow and whose row the verse means is unstated; the last item, the king's army, sets the list at court. The close, கடைபோக வாழ்தும், makes the rules a means of survival rather than a virtue.

items.claim: walking along in a row is avoided
standing on another's shadow is avoided
speaking into the middle of another's talk to pick at it is avoided
doing what the town resents is avoided
even the size of the king's army is not told

84.reading: The verse names four things that bring harm if one slights them, thinking them young, weak or familiar: the snake that lives in a hole, the king, fire, and the lion that lives in a cave.
84.nuance: The three reasons for contempt (இளைய, எளிய, பயின்றன) map loosely onto the four things: a young king, a small fire, a snake or lion one has grown used to. The king sits second, among beasts and fire, so his claim to respect is his power to harm.

items.claim: the snake in its hole harms one who slights it as small or familiar
the king harms one who slights him as young or familiar
fire harms one who slights it as small
the lion in its cave harms one who slights it as familiar

85.reading: The verse says that capable men, even when their charity, weddings, enterprise and houses grow very great, do nothing that outdoes the king, and that if they do, their lasting wealth is ruined.
85.domain_note: a wealthy subject of the king
85.nuance: Even அறம் is under the limit: a subject's giving must not outshine the king's. The rule is prudential, with ruin of wealth as its sanction.

items.claim: charity, however great, is not made to outdo the king's
a wedding is not made grander than the king's
enterprise is not pushed beyond the king's
the house is not built above the king's

86.reading: The verse says that one does not ask elders and superiors what they have eaten, does not change countenance on meeting them wherever they are met, and does not ask even mean people what they have eaten.
86.nuance: The question 'what did you eat' is barred upward and downward alike: புல்லரையும் extends the courtesy to the lowly. The syntax of lines 1-2 is loose; the reading takes குரவரை மிக்காரை as the object of both clauses.

items.claim: asking elders and superiors what they have eaten is avoided
turning one's mind or face on meeting them is avoided
even mean people are not asked what they have eaten

87.reading: The verse says that people do not wash the feet of one lying down, do not put flowers on him, never smear him with sandal paste even by oversight, and do not stand on the cot where someone lies.
87.nuance: Washing the feet, laying flowers and anointing with sandal are acts done to a body laid out in death, so the rule most likely keeps the living sleeper from being treated as a corpse; the verse does not say so. கட்டின் மிசை is read as the cot.

items.claim: the feet of one lying down are not washed
flowers are not put on one lying down
sandal paste is never smeared on one lying down, even by oversight
one does not stand on the cot where someone lies

norm.note: a rule of the period barring toward the sleeping the acts of the funeral rite

88.reading: The verse says that those who mean to live in the right way do not speak of the return on help they gave, do not find fault with food, and do not marvel at their own charity and the vows they kept.
88.nuance: All three are faults of the tongue about one's own goods: help given, food set before one, merit earned. Faulting food sits between the two boasts, so ingratitude to the host is grouped with self-praise.

items.claim: the fruit of help one has given is not spoken of
food is not found fault with
one's own charity and kept vows are not admired aloud

89.reading: The verse says that those of true vision do not want what cannot be had, do not grieve over what has passed, and are not troubled at heart by a hardship that has come beyond their power to prevent.
89.nuance: Each item is scoped: only the unattainable, only the past, only the trouble கைவாரா, beyond one's hand. The verse does not counsel calm before everything, only before what cannot be changed, and calls that calm a matter of vision (மெய்யாய காட்சி) rather than of will.

items.claim: what cannot be attained is not wanted
what has passed is not grieved over
a hardship beyond one's control does not distress the mind

90.reading: The verse says that people do not take up flowers already worn on the head or wear flowers already smelled, do not accept a cow from a brahmin's hand when one is given, and never hold out leavings to the புலை.
90.nuance: புலை is a caste term for the outcaste, set here as one to whom even leavings are not held out, so the rule bars a contact through food; it could also be read as an impure thing, hence the doubt. The cow rule is unclear: it may bar taking back a cow from a brahmin, as brahmins receive and do not give.

items.claim: flowers already worn on the head are not taken up
flowers already smelled are not worn
a cow is not taken from a brahmin's hand when given
leavings are not held out to the outcaste

norm.note: rules of the period on used flowers and leavings, with a birth-group barred even from receiving leavings and brahmins set apart as receivers

91.reading: The verse says that a thick wrap worn over the body, a stiffly raised neck and the noise of the feet are blamed even in the forest, since there are always those older than oneself.
91.nuance: The reason, தம்மின் மூத்த உள, makes the rule hold where no one is watching: even in the forest there are elders, perhaps the old trees and beings of the forest themselves. தாளிசைப்பு is read as the sound of the feet; it may be crossing the legs.

items.claim: a thick wrap over the body is blamed
a stiffly raised neck is blamed
noisy footsteps are blamed

92.reading: The verse says that when one performs an important auspicious rite one never fixes the day by asking the புலையர், and that one acts on the word of the unfailing அந்தணர், whose word never errs.
92.nuance: புலையர் and அந்தணர் are set as two birth-groups whose word on the day is untrusted and trusted; புலையர் is a caste term for the outcaste and here names persons, not a thing. That the புலையர் could be asked at all implies they were reckoners of days in the period.

norm.note: a rule of the period on who may fix the day of a rite, by birth-group

93.reading: The verse says that people do not stand and bustle in the public square, do not go about smeared with dirt, never speak harsh words, and do not go to a place where two stand together.
93.nuance: The last item guards a private talk from intrusion; the first keeps one from making a show in the common square. உஞற்றார் is read as 'do not exert or bustle'.

items.claim: bustling while standing in the public square is avoided
going about smeared with dirt is avoided
harsh words are never spoken
a place where two stand together is not approached

94.reading: The verse says that those of clear vision do not point with the hand while speaking, do not write with the foot, do not compare the poor with the rich by pointing at them, and do not sit while receiving what elders hand them.
94.nuance: The third item makes a comparison of rich and poor a discourtesy to the poor, not only to the rich. கால்மேல் எழுத்திடார் is obscure: writing with the toe, or writing on the leg.

items.claim: pointing with the hand while speaking is avoided
writing with or on the foot is avoided
the poor are not compared with the rich by pointing
what elders hand over is not received sitting

95.reading: The verse names four things to be guarded like gold and used with care, one's own body, one's wife, a deposit placed in one's keeping, and wealth set aside for one's own life, and says that failing to do so brings lasting harm.
95.nuance: The wife stands between the body and a deposit held in trust, so she is listed among goods in the man's keeping; the deposit, another's property, is guarded as closely as one's own body.

items.claim: one's own body is to be guarded like gold
one's wife is to be guarded like gold
a deposit placed in one's keeping is to be guarded like gold
wealth set aside for one's own life is to be guarded like gold

norm.note: a rule of the period that lists the wife among the goods a man guards

96.reading: The verse says that ஆசாரம் comes in any case to those who, like the ant, the weaver bird and the crow, hold fast to their own good work and strive to keep it in that manner.
96.nuance: The creatures are named without their qualities, so the model is their steady keeping to their own work. நந்தெறும்பு may be one word, 'the good ant', or two, the snail and the ant; it is taken as one item.

items.claim: the ant (or the snail and the ant) is a model of holding to one's own work
the weaver bird is a model of holding to one's own work
the crow is a model of holding to one's own work

97.reading: The verse says that before the great one says nothing except with folded hands or a covered mouth, and that speaking while looking into their eyes is a fault.
97.nuance: The last line can also be read as an instruction to speak looking at them; the reading takes பழி as naming the direct gaze a fault. The verse is missing from one of the source texts.

98.reading: The verse says that those who are not fools do not enter the gamblers' hall or the ground where the din never stops, and that one who enters them meets many harms.
98.nuance: The danger is in the place, not only the play: entering is the fault, and the noisy ground is ranked with the gaming hall.

items.claim: the gamblers' hall is not entered by the wise
the ground of unceasing din is not entered by the wise

99.reading: The verse says that those of steady vision do not look at the pounding place, the kitchen or the women there, do not raise their voices, and do not enter the house.
99.nuance: The pounding place and the kitchen are where the women of a house work, so the bar on looking is a bar on looking at women at their work; the verse ends by keeping the visitor out of the house altogether.

items.claim: the pounding place is not looked at
the kitchen is not looked at
women are not looked at
the voice is not raised
the house is not entered

norm.note: a rule of the period keeping a man's eyes off women and their working spaces in another's house

100.reading: The verse names nine who, rightly spoken of, are freed from ஆசாரம்: one from an unknown land, the destitute, the old, the young, one who has lost a life, the frightened, one who has eaten, one who has put the king's work first, and the bridegroom.
100.nuance: The code closes by bounding itself: the stranger who cannot know the local rule, those too weak or too young, those in fear or grief, and those taken up by the king's work or by their own wedding. உயிரிழந்தான் most likely means one bereaved by a death, though it can read as one near death.

items.claim: one from an unknown land is freed from ஆசாரம்
the destitute is freed from it
the old man is freed from it
the young are freed from it
one who has lost a life, most likely the bereaved, is freed from it
the frightened is freed from it
one who has eaten is freed from it
one who has put the king's work first is freed from it
the bridegroom is freed from it

norm.note: a rule of the period naming who is exempt from the rules of conduct

links.note: Kural 695 tells the king's servant not to listen in or press after secrets; Acharakkovai 81 names the palace places, the back gate, the assembly and the women's quarters, where looking in is barred, and exempts those whose office lies there.
links.teaches: Together they show that the courtier's discretion is spatial as well as verbal: what the Kural states as restraint of curiosity the Acharakkovai maps onto doors and rooms, and ties to office rather than to trust.
links.list_adds: It turns a general rule about secrets into three named places and adds the exception for those whose work lies there.

links.note: Kural 700 warns that intimacy which, presuming on old ties, does what is improper brings ruin; Acharakkovai 82 applies the same warning to sitting near the women, even with great intimacy (மிகக்கிழமை).
links.teaches: The pair show the period's fear of presumed closeness reaching its sharpest point in the women's place, where the Acharakkovai grounds the bar not in the king's anger but in a claim about women's changing liking.
links.list_adds: It names the one occasion where even the closest intimacy gives no right and adds a reason drawn from women rather than from the ruler.

links.note: Acharakkovai 83 says those who would live long do not tell the size of the king's army; in Patitruppattu 77 the poet, asked by travellers how large Poraiyan's army is, says he could not count it and describes its elephants.
links.teaches: Read together, the courtier's rule of silence and the bard's praise give the same answer to the same question: no figure is told, and the bard turns the forbidden number into the uncountable.

links.note: Kural 698 says the king is not to be slighted as young or as kin; Acharakkovai 84 sets the king among the snake, fire and the lion and says slighting any of them as young, weak or familiar brings harm.
links.teaches: The Kural asks respect for the light the king stands in, while the Acharakkovai asks it because he can harm, so the pair show two grounds for the same deference, the office and the danger.
links.list_adds: It ranks the king with a snake, fire and a lion, so his claim to respect is made one with their power to harm.

links.note: Thirikadugam 42 says the vellala family behaves toward brahmins as toward fire even when familiar with them; Acharakkovai 84 says fire, like the king, harms one who slights it as familiar.
links.teaches: The two books use one image, fire that burns the familiar, for two superiors, the brahmin and the king, showing that the period's rule against contempt bred by familiarity covered ritual and political rank alike.

links.note: Kural 692 says not desiring what kings desire brings lasting prosperity through them; Acharakkovai 85 says that even great charity, weddings, enterprise and houses must not outdo the king's, or lasting wealth (மன்னிய செல்வம்) is lost.
links.teaches: The pairing turns the Kural's general restraint into a ceiling on display, and shows that in the period even a subject's virtue, charity included, could not be allowed to outshine the king.
links.list_adds: It names four kinds of display, charity first among them, so the limit is placed on virtue as well as on luxury.

links.note: Kural 103 praises help given by those who do not weigh the return; Acharakkovai 88 says those who would live rightly do not even speak of the return on help they gave.
links.teaches: The Kural's giver does not reckon the return before giving; the Acharakkovai adds that he does not mention it after, so the pair carry the refusal to weigh from the act into speech.
links.list_adds: It groups silence about one's help with not faulting food and not praising one's own vows, so the rule becomes part of a discipline of the tongue about one's own goods.

links.note: Kural 379 asks why those who welcome good fortune grieve at bad, on the ground of fate; Acharakkovai 89 says those of true vision do not grieve over what has passed or what is beyond their control.
links.teaches: The Kural grounds calm in fate, whereas the Acharakkovai limits it to the unattainable, the past and the uncontrollable and grounds it in vision, so the pair show calm resting either on what governs events or on seeing which events one can still change.
links.list_adds: It splits the Kural's single good and bad fortune into three cases, each scoped to what cannot be changed.

links.note: Acharakkovai 90 sets rules toward the பார்ப்பார், from whose hand a cow is not taken, and the புலை, to whom leavings are not held out; Sivavakkiyar asks what a Paraiyar woman and a Brahmin woman are, since no mark on flesh, skin or bone divides them.
links.teaches: Read against each other, the rule that ranks two birth-groups by what may pass between their hands meets a denial that the body carries any rank, so the purity rule is shown to depend on a mark the Siddhar says is not there.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 4 says a proud raised neck (ஏக்கழுத்தம்) in one who has nothing to be proud of draws the laughter of the good; Acharakkovai 91 says a raised neck (ஏக்கழுத்து) is blamed even in the forest, since there are always those older than oneself.
links.teaches: Sirupanchamoolam faults the raised neck when it lacks ground, but the Acharakkovai faults it anywhere, even unseen, so the pair separate pride as absurdity from pride as disrespect to elders.

links.note: Naladiyar 52 calls those who prattle endlessly (தொலைவில்லா) of grammar and astrology the greatest fools; Acharakkovai 92 tells one to fix the day of a rite from the unfailing (தொலைவில்லா) அந்தணர், whose word never errs.
links.teaches: The same word, தொலைவில்லா, marks the Naladiyar's endless and foolish astrology and the Acharakkovai's unfailing reckoners, so the two books take opposite views of consulting the day before acting.
links.list_adds: It sets the reckoning of days in a contrast between two birth-groups, so the question becomes whose reckoning to trust, not whether to reckon.

links.note: Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous, kind to every living being; Acharakkovai 92 trusts the word of the அந்தணர் and distrusts that of the புலையர் on the day of a rite.
links.teaches: The Kural derives the name அந்தணர் from conduct, while the Acharakkovai uses it as a birth-group set against the புலையர், so the pair show the same word serving as a moral title in one book and a caste rank in the other.
links.list_adds: It pairs the அந்தணர் with the புலையர் as opposites, a contrast of birth that the Kural's definition by kindness does not make.

links.note: Kural 57 asks what use the guarding of women by confinement is, since the best guard is their own steadfastness; Acharakkovai 95 lists the wife among four things a man guards like gold.
links.teaches: The Kural moves the guard of a wife inside her, while the Acharakkovai keeps it in the husband's hands beside his body and his deposits, so the pair show two views of where a wife's keeping lies.
links.list_adds: It puts the wife in one list with the man's body, a deposit and his savings, so she is guarded as a possession.

links.note: Thirikadugam 62 names the man who wrongly keeps a deposit placed with him as one who loses his line; Acharakkovai 95 lists a deposit among four things to be guarded like gold.
links.teaches: One verse says what keeping a deposit asks and the other what breaking it costs, and together they show the deposit as another's property that the period held as close as one's own body and family.

links.note: Acharakkovai 1 names eight virtues as the seed from which ஆசாரம் grows; Acharakkovai 96 says ஆசாரம் comes in any case to those who hold to their own work like the ant, the weaver bird and the crow.
links.teaches: The book that opened by rooting conduct in inner virtues nears its close by rooting it in diligence, so ஆசாரம் is given two sources, character and steady work, and the second is learned from animals.

links.note: Kural 694 tells one to suppress whispers and shared smiles in the presence of the great; Acharakkovai 97 says one speaks before the great only with folded hands or a covered mouth and does not look into their eyes.
links.teaches: The Kural forbids the small private signs that the great may read as against them, and the Acharakkovai prescribes the posture of the mouth, hands and eyes, so together they show restraint before the great as a whole bodily discipline.
links.list_adds: It names the hands, the mouth and the eyes in turn, so the Kural's ban on two signs becomes a full posture of address.

links.note: Elathi 12 says it is good neither to desire nor to look at five places, among them the killing ground and the ground where men gamble; Acharakkovai 98 says the wise do not enter the gamblers' hall or the ground of unceasing din, and that entering brings harm.
links.teaches: Both books treat the gambling place as a place to avoid, but the Jain Elathi bars even desiring or seeing it alongside the killing ground, while the Acharakkovai bars entering it for the harm it brings, so the pair show a moral and a prudential reason for the same avoidance.

links.note: Acharakkovai 1 makes eight virtues the seed of ஆசாரம்; Acharakkovai 100, the last verse, names nine persons freed from it: the stranger, the destitute, the old, the young, the bereaved, the frightened, one who has eaten, one on the king's work and the bridegroom.
links.teaches: Read as the book's frame, the pair show the code bounded at both ends: it grows from virtues that bind everyone, but its rules lapse for those whom ignorance, weakness, fear, grief or duty prevent from keeping them.

links.note: Elathi 35 promises kingship to one who feeds the renouncers, the powerless, the unknown, the dead or bereaved (இறந்தார்), the destitute and the young; Acharakkovai 100 frees from ஆசாரம் the stranger, the destitute, the old, the young and one who has lost a life.
links.teaches: The two books name nearly the same weak persons, but the Elathi makes them claims on the giver's food while the Acharakkovai lifts the rules of conduct from them, so the vulnerable are owed help in one code and excused in the other.

source_issues: Verse 82 line 1 reads மகளிரி, most likely மகளிர் miswritten.
Verse 81 line 3 reads தொழிற்குரிவர், most likely தொழிற்குரியவர்.
Verse 91 line 2 பழித்தாரமாம் is unclear; read as 'are blamed'.
Verse 96 line 1 நந்தெறும்பு may be one word or two (the snail and the ant), so the creature count is three or four.
Verse 97 is missing from one of the source texts (the tool flags site_diff); its last line is hard to construe.
Verse 100 counts nine (ஒன்பதின்மர்); உயிரிழந்தான் is obscure.
